title: Gregory the Great
hookLine: a pope who called himself servant of the servants of God

lines: A LETTER OPENS WITH A TITLE.
THE POPE WHO WROTE DOWN BENEDICT.
SERVANT OF THE SERVANTS OF GOD.
cards: Old letters open with a name and a title. Dear Sir. From the Office of the Director.
Titles tell you where someone stands. The man who wrote down Scholastica's storm was a bishop of Rome, a pope, and he signed his letters with a title of his own choosing. Not lord of the church.
Not head of anything. He called himself servant of the servants of God. It was harder to live than to write.

teach.h: A MONK WHO LOVED THE QUIET.
teach.b: His name was Gregory, and later Christians called him the Great. Before he was pope, he had been a monk. He turned his family's house in Rome into a monastery, and he loved the quiet there.

Then he was made bishop of Rome, and the quiet ended. Bede passes on Gregory's own complaint: the cares of his office pulled his mind away from prayer, like a ship tossed in a storm, looking back at the shore it had left.
So he knew what the job could do to a person.

teach.h: THE PASTORAL RULE: BEWARE OF PRIDE.
teach.b: He wrote a whole book about it, the Pastoral Rule, a guide for anyone who leads souls. One of its warnings is that the person at the top is in special danger of pride.
And the title: Servus servorum Dei, servant of the servants of God. It echoes what Jesus told his friends when two of them asked for the places of honor beside him.
In Mark's Gospel he says, "whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all." Gregory put that at the top of his letters, where everyone would see it, including him.
Christians remember him in different ways. Catholics count him among the great popes and teachers of the church.
Orthodox Christians honor him too, as Saint Gregory the Dialogist, after the book where Benedict's story is told. And a thread for tomorrow: Gregory is the one who sent monks to England.

teach.h: A TITLE IS A PUBLIC PROMISE.
teach.b: A title is a promise made in public. His said: I'm here to serve those who serve God.

how: Catholics honor Gregory the Great as a pope and Doctor of the Church, and Orthodox Christians honor him as Saint Gregory the Dialogist; the plainchant called Gregorian chant is named after him by tradition.

games.q: you're a monk who loves the quiet of the monastery. you're made bishop of Rome, and the quiet is over. what do you do?
o: refuse and stay in the monastery.
take it, and choose a title that keeps you low.
take it, and leave the monastery behind for good.
games.why: Gregory took up the office, grieved the lost quiet, and signed himself servant of the servants of God.

practice: Think of the people who make your day work and rarely get thanked: whoever cleans the building, drives the bus, answers the phones, stocks the shelves.
Pick one, imagine what their day is like, and find one small way to serve them back: learning their name, a proper thank-you, a job made easier by a minute. If you pray, pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Gregory. The monk who became pope, later called the Great, and signed himself servant of the servants of God.
